title: Issue 1 Cover — The Weight of Dead Iron
summary: Sell Issue 1 through the discovery that an ordinary industrial excavation has reached something impossibly deliberate beneath the geology. The cover promises buried history and recognition without showing Starbreaker, Redlin, the full Desert Marker, or the memory rupture.
settingText: Olyria-Prime excavation trench at shift end. Black bedrock, practical amber-white work lights, drill machinery, ladders and ordinary industrial clutter. Deep in the cut, the drill has stopped against one unnaturally smooth manufactured black edge exposed beneath fractured natural stone. Night and a sparse star field above.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-BLEED COVER IMAGE. Use a steep vertical composition looking down into the Olyria trench. Theo is a small but unmistakable human figure beside the halted drill at the bottom third of the image; the impossible manufactured edge beneath the rock is the second focal anchor.

The visual contradiction must read instantly: everything around the object is rough geology and worksite improvisation; the exposed edge is mathematically deliberate, ancient and physically real. Do not show the full Desert Marker shape. Do not add glow as a substitute for wrongness.
Make Theo's posture carry recognition before explanation: he is not triumphantly discovering treasure; he is staring at something he somehow expected to find.

Reserve the upper 20–25 percent as a clean, high-contrast masthead field using dark sky, controlled stars and minimal machinery intrusion. Keep the issue title readable without covering Theo or the exposed edge.
THUMBNAIL READ: small human figure + deep trench + one razor-straight black manufactured seam under stone. The eye should understand 'buried impossible thing' before reading any title.
SPOILER CEILING: no Starbreaker, no Redlin, no ancient battlefield, no full Marker silhouette, no supernatural memory overlay, no Rae archive evidence, no Adrian reveal.

title: Issue 2 Cover — Glass Dust and Violet Light
summary: Sell Issue 2 through the fact that the ancient conflict had two coherent, personally familiar sides rather than a clean hero/villain split. Starbreaker and Redlin approach the same catastrophe with opposite visual and moral instincts while Mero remains the human scale between them.
settingText: Ancient Desert Marker battlefield in the suspended moment before catastrophic escalation. Ruined terrain and violet particulate light hang in the air; the decisive detonation itself has not happened.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-BLEED COVER IMAGE. Build a strong diagonal opposition rather than a face-off poster. Starbreaker occupies one side in fractured white-gold-black radiance; Redlin occupies the other in dark enclosed armor with deep red containment channels. Both reach toward the same unstable central phenomenon rather than pointing weapons at each other.

Their gestures should reveal philosophy through action: Starbreaker's hand/weapon commits force forward; Redlin's body and containment hardware close around the danger. Neither expression is villainous. Both look exhausted and certain enough to be dangerous.
General Mero appears much smaller at human scale in the lower middle distance, physically between the two systems of power and trying to keep the situation from becoming irreversible.
Use suspended violet glass-like dust and light as connective atmosphere, not generic magic. Keep bodies readable and distinct from effects.
Reserve the masthead zone with controlled negative space above the diagonal clash. Preserve the Issue 1 trade-dress proportions exactly from the pixel-read reference.
THUMBNAIL READ: white-gold open fracture versus red-black containment around one central danger, with one small human between them.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show the decisive detonation, casualties from it, Theo/Rae ancient identities, Flux, Arbiter, or the Reset.

title: Issue 3 Cover — The Architecture of Ruin
summary: Sell Issue 3 through the physical persistence of forgotten war inside ordinary civilian life: a buried dreadnought surfaces through contemporary Vael-Tor while people, luggage, transit and rescue remain the scale reference.
settingText: Present-day Vael-Tor civilian transit/port district in rain. Wet glass, concourses, apartments, service vehicles, luggage, vendors and maintenance infrastructure occupy the foreground while ancient black dreadnought structure physically emerges through newer construction.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-BLEED COVER IMAGE. Compose the city at human eye level first: civilians and refugees moving through a rain-wet concourse, Theo and Rae helping direct or carry people, Adrian nearby. Behind and beneath them, the enormous black geometry of the buried dreadnought has broken through ordinary architecture.

The dreadnought must feel physically embedded in the city rather than hovering as a cool spaceship reveal. New walls, transit structures and utility runs should visibly have been built over and around its forgotten mass.

Atlas appears only as a restrained ancient-memory counter-image integrated into one structural plane or reflected rain surface: monumental, deep blue-black and gold, holding impossible weight. He must not become the foreground poster subject.
Keep civilians larger and more numerous than military imagery. The issue is about who bears the consequence when history returns.
Reserve upper architecture/sky for the stable masthead. Do not let ship geometry slice through the logo readability zone.
THUMBNAIL READ: ordinary inhabited city + impossible black hull erupting through it + small people still trying to move one another to safety.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show the dreadnought fully operational, any ultimate institutional response, ancient Theo/Rae, or the later identity reveal.

title: Issue 4 Cover — Silence in the Vault
summary: Sell Issue 4 through a room that remembers more than the protagonists do. The black treaty table anchors both present civic ruin and an ancient impossible decision, but the cover must not reveal Theo or Rae's former roles.
settingText: Pax-Aeterna treaty vault/civic chamber. Severe human-scale stone architecture, a long black treaty table, open doors and galleries that once looked directly onto evacuation concourses. Present-day quiet occupies the room while an ancient layer is visible only through controlled reflection.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-BLEED COVER IMAGE. Make the black treaty table the dominant shape, beginning large in the foreground and narrowing toward the present-day Theo, Rae and Adrian entering at the far end.

In the polished table surface only, allow a restrained ancient reflection: Arbiter in her severe judicial silhouette at one end, exhausted evacuation activity visible through the old open doors behind her. The reflection should feel like the room retaining a decision, not a supernatural ghost scene.
Do not reflect ancient Theo or ancient Rae. Their presence in the past is the issue's midpoint reveal and must remain unspoiled.
The table should divide the image without turning it into symmetrical courtroom cliché. Empty chairs and worn civic architecture should imply that decisions outlast the people who made them.
Use upper wall/doorway negative space for the masthead; keep the trade dress legible against quiet stone rather than effects.
THUMBNAIL READ: enormous black civic table + tiny present trio + one severe ancient reflection.
SPOILER CEILING: no ancient Theo/Rae, no explicit extinction act, no midpoint dialogue reveal, no Reset machinery or imagery.

title: Issue 5 Cover — Embers of the Zenith
summary: Sell Issue 5 through autobiographical continuity returning: Theo and Rae now know they were inside the ancient institutions, and the frightening question is no longer whether the memories are real but what choices they personally made.
settingText: Present-day institutional/ruin threshold that can visually align with remembered ancient architecture without becoming a portal. Controlled split of present tactile surfaces and damaged ancient depth.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-BLEED COVER IMAGE. Theo and Rae stand in present-day clothing as the clear foreground figures. Their cast shadows fall across the ground/wall and align precisely with their already-revealed ancient roles: Theo's shadow stands just behind Mero's human command silhouette; Rae's shadow stands beside Arbiter's recording position.
The shadows must read as recovered self-continuity, not possession, alternate-universe doubles or ghost costumes. Present Theo and Rae remain fully themselves.

Afterlight appears in the damaged distance performing material restoration on a devastated inhabited environment: white-gold living repair motifs, exhausted rather than saintly. She is the issue's new promise, not the dominant cover subject.
Use one ember-like warm restoration field against cooler present architecture to justify the issue title without bathing the cover in orange.
Preserve a clean masthead zone and the exact Issue 1 trade-dress proportions.
THUMBNAIL READ: two present people whose shadows unmistakably belong inside the ancient world behind them.
SPOILER CEILING: do not reveal Theo's missing opinion to Mero, Rae's unfinished answer to Arbiter, the Reset choice, or Issue 8 positions.

title: Issue 6 Cover — The Margin of Error
summary: Sell Issue 6 through memory escaping the protagonists and entering ordinary public life. Flux embodies unbearable uncertainty while a mundane transit worker experiences a recovered relationship that current reality cannot verify.
settingText: Present-day Tyrellis transit platform or equivalent ordinary public transit space: practical signage shapes without readable environmental text, work radios, commuters, worn seating and arriving trains. Black-violet probability fracture intrudes with controlled precision.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-BLEED COVER IMAGE. Put an ordinary transit worker in the foreground as the emotional center even though the worker is not a reusable character shelf entry: adult worker in practical uniform, work radio in hand, turning toward an empty place beside him with sudden recognition and grief. Do not add an invented name or text.

Flux occupies the secondary visual layer across platform glass and structural reflections: one readable body with several offset black-violet silhouettes and prismatic seams, suggesting incompatible possible continuities without becoming a decorative magic cloud.

Theo and Rae may appear small in the middle distance observing that the problem has moved beyond them. Rae's body language should already lean toward protective caution; do not stage her as authoritarian.
Use platform geometry and repeated rails/doors to create multiple routes that almost align but do not. No holographic probability equations.
Keep a stable dark-to-light masthead field above the platform and preserve trade-dress geometry from Issue 1.
THUMBNAIL READ: grieving ordinary worker + empty place + fractured violet human silhouette repeated in glass.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show Flux's disappearance explanation, later Neo-Vectra policy, Oryon, the final council, or the Reset mechanism.

title: Issue 7 Cover — Gravity and Consequence
summary: Sell Issue 7 through the moment protective caution hardens into identity-based control. The emotional subject is a current couple being separated by recovered-history policy while Rae recognizes the coercive structure she helped create.
settingText: Present-day Neo-Vectra civic/transit route during temporary security measures. Ordinary barriers, queues, bags, keys and current-life possessions. No riot spectacle.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-BLEED COVER IMAGE. Center a recurring present-day couple on opposite sides of a temporary transparent security barrier. They reach or lean toward one another while still carrying the ordinary bags/keys of their shared current life. Their separation, not violence, is the immediate emotional hook.

Rae stands on the policy/authority side of the barrier, slightly behind the line she helped justify, looking at the couple rather than at Theo or Adrian. Her face should register recognition that protection has become classification.

Oryon appears only in the barrier's reflective/structural visual layer: pale controlled silhouette with precise predictive geometry that maps routes and threat paths across the transparent divider. His system should visually resemble a cage without turning him into a villain.
Theo and Adrian can remain small supporting figures beyond Rae, present enough to anchor series continuity but not competing for focus.
Keep the masthead zone visually clean and do not allow security signage or generated environmental text into it.
THUMBNAIL READ: two people separated by one transparent line, Rae standing on the side that drew it, predictive geometry tightening around the barrier.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show Rae dismantling the policy, Adrian's admission that the Reset began as temporary, the final Core-Forge confrontation, or Kyn.

title: Issue 8 Cover — The Shape of Tomorrow
summary: Sell the finale through the unresolved question of authority over memory. Theo, Rae and Adrian occupy different positions around the physical scar of the Reset while ancient geometry aligns behind them; nobody has acted yet and the outcome remains unknown.
settingText: Present-day Core-Forge central scar chamber where repaired modern construction and monumental ancient foundations align in the same physical geometry. The scar is materially legible but not a glowing control device.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-BLEED COVER IMAGE. Compose Theo, Rae and Adrian as a tense triangle around the physical scar of the Reset. Theo and Adrian each occupy a different route toward the scar; Rae occupies the third axis between them, not yet physically stopping either one.
Their hands and body positions should suggest three competing relationships to the same history without depicting the decisive gestures from the issue. No one touches or activates anything.

Ancient architectural geometry aligns exactly behind the present chamber, allowing the reader to feel past and present occupying the same ground. Kyn appears in a restrained ancient layer seated or standing quietly off-axis, exhausted and humanly attentive rather than mystical.
Do not depict the full ancient council, Mero authorizing the Reset, ancient Adrian performing it, Rae's final interruption, aftermath vignettes, or the missing-stars image.
Use the central scar as the strongest geometric anchor below the masthead, with clean upper negative space preserving the established trade dress.
THUMBNAIL READ: three present people around one irreversible scar, ancient geometry perfectly aligned behind them.
SPOILER CEILING: no final choice, no 'Nobody chooses for everyone again' staging, no missing stars, no Flux/Regent explanation, no Season 2 tease.
